newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Bank supervisors launch first global principles.
newsitem.headline: Bank supervisors launch first global principles.

text.p: Banking regulators worldwide have for the first time agreed on the basic principles of supervision as part of international efforts to strengthen financial stability worldwide, especially in emerging countries.

The 25 Basle Core Principles represent a strong and detailed response by central bankers and supervisors to policy makers, who called for upgrading banking standards in emerging countries in the wake of Mexico's financial crisis in late 1994.
The principles were drawn up by the Basle Committee on Banking Supervision, which represents the Group of 10 (G10) industrial nations, and supervisors from 15 emerging countries.
It is the first truly global effort by bank supervisors to create a worldwide standard -- a Supervisors' Charter -- that argues for their independence, resource, power and authority.

Although many of the principles are standard supervisory practice, the political implications will be far-reaching in some countries where connected lending is commonplace and governments influence banks' lending decisions.
Supervisors can draw on the considerable moral weight of a globally-accepted document when arguing for legal changes.

The document, released on Tuesday by the Basle Committtee, is being sent out for consultation in the hope that a final version can be presented to the September annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in Hong Kong.
The principles will also be discussed by the Group of Seven (G7) leading industrial nations at their June summit in Denver.
At the previous summit in Lyon, G7 heads of state sought swift action to improve emerging market banking supervision.

Policy makers put the spotlight on banking supervision following Mexico's crisis. With economies increasingly interdependent and with huge capital flows, disruption to local banking systems poses a risk to the entire international financial system.

But the report counters the notion that Mexico's crisis was caused by poor banking. Banking supervision is only part of policies to promote financial stability and the foundation of a stable financial system is sound macro-economic policies.
"Providing sound and sustainable macro-economic policies are not within the competence of banking supervisors," it said.
Central bankers expect the IMF and World Bank to draw on the principles as part of their more wide-ranging work to improve macroeconomic stability.

The principles go far beyond the traditional scope of the G10-dominated Basle Committee, best known for its 1988 Capital Accord on capital adequacy and devising rules for consolidated reporting, disclosure and derivatives.
Emerging countries, however, often face far more basic shortcomings in their banking sector.
The principles endorse minimum capital standards that should reflect risks and internationally-active banks should fulfill the requirements of the Capital Accord.
"Supervisors should consider requiring higher than minimum capital ratios when it appears appropriate due to the particular risk profile of the bank...," the report said.

The report outlines the basic elements of an effective supervisory system, including its preconditions such as sound macro-economic policies, business laws that are enforced, well-defined accounting principles that are internationally accepted, independent audits, supervision of other markets, an efficient payment system and effective market discipline.
The preconditions include giving supervisors enough powers "to effect an efficient resolution of problems in banks."
Other principles discuss bank licensing and structure, regulations and requirements, methods, information requirements, formal powers of supervisors and cross-border banking.
The G10 comprises 11 countries, the G7 -- the U.S., Japan, Canada, Germany, Britain, France and Italy -- as well the Netherlands, Belgium, Sweden and Switzerland.

The 15 emerging countries that helped create the principles are Chile, China, Czech Republic, Hong Kong, Mexico, Russia, Thailand, Brazil, Hungary, India, Indonesia, Korea, Malaysia, Poland and Singapore.
